summary:
blinkX is an interactive, browser-based blink comparator and quick-look science viewer built for NASA's SPHEREx mission. Users enter an object name or sky coordinates and watch SPHEREx Level 2 exposures across all six infrared bands (0.75–5.0 µm) align north-up and play like a movie—making moving stars, brown dwarfs, asteroids, and variable stars immediately stand out.

Instead of bulk downloads, blinkX fetches only the needed pixel rows on demand from NASA's public AWS SPHEREx mirror and IRSA cutout services, combining SPHEREx epochs with historical WISE (2010) and 2MASS (~2000) reference frames so sub-pixel proper motion becomes unmistakable. Beyond visual blinking and difference imaging (Subtract B − A), users can inspect multi-band spectra and light curves, overlay Gaia DR3 stars propagated to each observation date, manually mark discoveries, and run a built-in motion engine that fits trajectories, classifies objects, and predicts future sky paths.
details:
What blinkX Does & How It Works

blinkX brings the classic astronomical blink comparator—historically used to discover Pluto—into a modern web app tailored to SPHEREx's 102-channel infrared all-sky survey:

1. Target & Archive Lookup: Resolves object names via SIMBAD (with automatic CfA and IDIA mirror fallbacks) or accepts ICRS RA/Dec coordinates, propagates catalog positions to the observation date using proper motion, and queries IRSA's SIA v2 and TAP services (spherex.plane + spherex.artifact) in parallel.

2. On-Demand Pixel Streaming (No Bulk Downloads): Rather than downloading full ~4 MB cutout files with large PSF tables, blinkX reads only the required image rows via HTTP byte-range requests from NASA's public AWS S3 mirror (nasa-irsa-spherex), falling back to partial-stream IRSA cutouts when needed. Cached per-detector WCS-WAVE tables shipped in spx/data give exact pixel wavelengths without downloading the trailing tables.

3. Alignment, Calibration & Stacking: Removes modeled zodiacal light (ZODI) and local sky background, reprojects exposures onto a common north-up 2× oversampled grid (3.1″ pixels vs. 6.15″ detector scale), groups observations into survey epochs, and computes inverse-variance weighted stacks while flagging saturated or corrupted pixels rather than hiding them.

4. Multi-Epoch & Multi-Survey Blinking: Prepends historical AllWISE (2010) and 2MASS (~1998–2001) cutouts to the timeline so sub-pixel SPHEREx proper motion (~4–5″ per epoch) turns into unmistakable multi-arcminute jumps.

5. Interactive Browser Sky Viewer & Motion Engine: A custom HTML5/Canvas component supports instant client-side stretch/brightness/contrast controls, linked side-by-side/swipe/difference comparison, Gaia DR3 overlays propagated to each frame's date, manual discovery marking, two-object relative motion comparison, joint trajectory fitting (still, drift, drift + parallax, curved) with leave-one-out consistency tests, object classification, uncertainty cones, and quick-look 6-band spectra & light curves (0.75–5.0 µm).

Benefits & Intended Impact

- Accessible Citizen Science & Education: Requires no astronomy background—includes five guided challenge presets (Barnard's Star, Epsilon Indi B, WISE 0855−0714, RW Aurigae, R Draconis), a 5-lesson interactive tutorial, optional discovery helpers, /RTP preloaded random sky exploration, and a bilingual English/Turkish interface.

- Fast Quick-Look Analysis for Researchers: Turns ~65-second archive fetches into ~7–10 second interactive sessions with shareable URL parameters, iframe embedding, GIF animations, and CSV exports.

Tools, Languages & Software Used

- Languages: Python 3.12, HTML5, CSS, JavaScript (custom two-way Streamlit component).

- Frameworks & Libraries: Streamlit, Astropy, Astroquery, Reproject, NumPy, SciPy, Pillow, Plotly, Requests, Pytest (synthetic offline test suite).

- Development Environment: Standard personal computers (Windows 11), Git/GitHub, and Streamlit Community Cloud-ready configuration.

Creativity & Key Design Considerations

- Solving Sub-Pixel Motion & Faint-Target Constraints: SPHEREx epochs are ~6 months apart, meaning even fast stars move less than one 6.15″ pixel between passes. We solved this with 2× oversampling, Subtract (B − A) difference imaging, centroid tracking, and automatic 2010 WISE / 2000 2MASS baseline frames.

- Resilience to Slow/Busy Archives: Built hedged parallel SIA+TAP queries, AWS byte-range fetching to avoid HTTP 503 throttling, disk caching, background prefetching across all six bands, and automatic mirror fallbacks (SIMBAD mirrors, VizieR fallback for Gaia DR3).

- Scientific Honesty: Saturated and flagged pixels (e.g., R Draconis, Barnard's Star) are clearly marked as hollow points/warnings rather than silently masked, and quick-look photometry links directly to the official IRSA Spectrophotometry Tool.


Live Web App: https://blinkx.streamlit.app
